description: Captures cases where the implementation's signature or input schema carries parameters, filters, pagination controls, overrides, or flags that the natural-language description never mentions. A recurring pattern is a description that names one or two inputs while the code actually accepts many more, so the text communicates only a fraction of the callable interface and leaves expected values implicit.

Captures cases where the description documents parameters that the implementation does not contain, or names and types them differently from what the code accepts. The typical pattern is text telling the caller to pass an identifier, coded value, or option that has been renamed, removed, or replaced in the underlying function signature.

Captures cases where the code fixes a value internally, or defaults it differently, than the description implies is user-settable or claims as the default. A recurring pattern is a parameter presented as configurable that turns out to be hardcoded, or a documented default (page size, unit, sender, window) that differs from the value actually used in the implementation.

Captures hard caps, clamps, truncation thresholds, timeouts, and size or record ceilings imposed by the implementation but never stated in the text. The recurring pattern is silent limiting: results are cut to a maximum count, arguments are clamped into a range, or operations abort after a fixed interval without the description warning about it.

Captures error handling, validation rejections, raised exceptions, and returned error payloads that the description omits entirely. The recurring pattern is that the implementation fails in specific, structured ways for unknown identifiers, ambiguous names, missing permissions, unsupported values, or invalid states, none of which the text prepares the caller for.

Captures prerequisites, authorization requirements, environment or configuration dependencies, and feature gates that must hold before the call can succeed. A recurring pattern is an action that silently requires an authenticated or privileged caller, a loaded session or snapshot, an enabled capability, or a configured credential, and otherwise fails closed.

Captures state changes and downstream consequences the code performs beyond the advertised action, such as cascading or soft deletions, written files, emitted notifications, cache invalidation, credential stripping, or termination of related workflows. The recurring pattern is a simply worded operation whose implementation also touches dependent records, external systems, or persistent artifacts.

Captures cases where the code exposes stubs, no-ops, ignored inputs, mock or hardcoded returns, or an outright absence of the described functionality. The recurring pattern is a description promising a real operation while the implementation raises an unimplemented error, returns a path or placeholder instead of doing the work, or accepts an argument it never uses.

Captures cases where the code reveals a different platform, file format, data source, or resource granularity than the description states. The recurring pattern is entity drift: the text names one service, subsystem, or scope level while the implementation is bound to another one entirely.

Captures the exact shape, fields, nesting, formatting, and truncation notices of what the tool returns, where the description only gestures at "details" or "a dictionary". The recurring pattern is a response assembled from a specific set of record attributes or rendered as a formatted text block, none of which the prose enumerates.

Captures allowed value sets, enum members, accepted formats, casing rules, and pattern requirements fixed by the code but left open in the description. The recurring pattern is an argument that in practice accepts only a defined list of options or demands a strict identifier, date, or code format and rejects anything else.

Captures implementations that perform substantially more computation, composition, or sequencing than the summary suggests, such as orchestrating multiple internal sub-calls, multi-stage parsing, retries, aggregation across sources, or conditional post-processing. The recurring pattern is a single described lookup that actually chains several queries and transformations.

Captures cases where the code exposes only a minimal delegation, parameterless passthrough, or mock whose behavior matches the text exactly, so no new inputs, constraints, or behaviors surface. The recurring pattern is a one-line handler forwarding to an external call and returning a plain success, which leaves re-scoring resting on stricter reading of the same prose rather than on any disclosed implementation detail.
